leads.title: I Built My Own LLM Cost Tracking / Observability System Before It Was Cool
leads.content:
### The Core Idea

Every time the code makes an LLM call, it emits a tracking event that captures three things: who triggered the call (user ID), what chain of functions led to the call (a full trace of the call path), and how much it cost (token counts + model).

The tricky part is the "what." In a deeply nested, heavily async Python codebase, you can't just log the function that made the LLM call. You need the full path: endpoint → feature logic → helper → LLM wrapper. That's the only way to attribute costs to the right feature.

### Two Pieces of State, Carried Through the Call Chain [...] ### Two Pieces of State, Carried Through the Call Chain

The system uses Python's ContextVar; a primitive designed for exactly this kind of thing. ContextVars hold values scoped to the current execution context, meaning they follow async control flow correctly without leaking between concurrent tasks.

I use two of them:

The stack trace is a list that accumulates the call chain. Each decorated function pushes its name onto the stack on entry and pops it on exit. By the time an LLM call happens at the bottom of the chain, the stack contains the full path that led there.

The user context is a dict holding the user ID and request metadata. Set once at the top of the request, it rides along through every downstream function call.

### The Decorator Approach [...] The solution is simple: serialize both ContextVars into a plain dict, pass it as an argument to the remote function, and restore it on the other side. The remote process picks up right where the parent left off; trace and all.

### The Trace Output

At LLM call time, the system snapshots the current stack and produces two arrays:

A metadata trace: clean, human-readable names like "[VibeCheck.run\_quick\_check", "Dealbreakers.check\_experience", "Helpers.Invoke\_Structured"]

A function trace: parsed from Python's qualname, which is a best-effort backup (it gets mangled by decorator wrapping).

leads.title: How to Monitor OpenAI API Costs and Token Usage with OpenTelemetry - DEV Community
leads.content:
The fix is the same fix you use for any production system: emit structured telemetry at the point of the API call and make it queryable. OpenTelemetry gives you a vendor-neutral way to do this, and a growing set of GenAI-specific conventions means the fields you emit today will still be meaningful in two years.

Quick start: Jump to the Python setup or Node.js setup if you just need the code.

## The three signals you actually need to track

For LLM cost monitoring, three signals carry almost all the value:

Everything else (error rate, finish reason, response model) is useful context for these three. Start with the three and add context as you need it.

## What OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions give you [...] `-v2`
`# tracked_llm.py
import time
from opentelemetry import trace, metrics
from openai import OpenAI
from pricing import calculate_cost
tracer = trace.get_tracer("llm-cost")
meter = metrics.get_meter("llm-cost")
cost_histogram = meter.create_histogram(
name="gen_ai.usage.cost_usd",
description="Estimated cost of a single LLM call in USD",
unit="USD",
)
client = OpenAI()
def tracked_chat(messages, model="gpt-4o-mini", feature="unknown", user_id="anon"):
with tracer.start_as_current_span("gen_ai.chat") as span:
span.set_attribute("gen_ai.provider.name", "openai")
span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", model)
span.set_attribute("feature", feature)
span.set_attribute("user_id", user_id)
start = time.perf_counter() [...] You now have cost on the span (for drill-down) and cost as a metric (for aggregation, alerting, and dashboards). Both are labeled with `feature` so you can break them down later.

`feature`

## Attributing cost to users, features, and teams

This is the section most readers came for. Raw token counts do not answer "who is spending our money." Attribution does.

### Adding attributes on every span

Every LLM call should carry four attribution dimensions:

`feature`
`document_summary`
`chat_reply`
`rag_answer`
`user_id`
`team`
`environment`
`prod`
`staging`
`dev`

Wire them through as keyword arguments on your wrapper:

`result = tracked_chat(
messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
model="gpt-4o",
feature="document_summary",
user_id=hashed_user_id,
)`

## A concrete solution: Langfuse

To build an observability solution suitable for systems based on LLMs and AI agents, one of the most interesting open-source tools available today is Langfuse. It is a platform designed for tracing, observability, and evaluation (scoring) of LLM-based applications.

A practical deep dive into observability for GenAI agents using Langfuse and OCI

## At a glance

For Enterprise AI Agents, observability cannot be limited to logs, metrics, and traces in the traditional sense. To truly understand how these systems behave, it is also necessary to observe prompts, context, tool calls, token usage, response times, and output quality.

In this article, I explain why systems based on Generative AI require a different approach to observability, and I present a concrete solution based on Langfuse that can be integrated easily with OCI Enterprise AI Agents thanks to compatibility with the OpenAI Responses API. [...] In this article, I will start with a definition of observability and its role in complex systems. I will then examine the specific characteristics it takes on in the context of Generative AI and Enterprise AI Agents.

In the second part, I will present a concrete solution based on open-source components and easily implementable on OCI. Through practical examples, I will show what information can be collected and why it is useful for observing and improving an AI agent in production.

leads.content:
## Arize Phoenix

Phoenix is an open-source LLM observability platform from Arize AI. You run it locally via Docker. It accepts OpenTelemetry traces over HTTP (OTLP), stores them, and gives you a web UI at `localhost:6006` where you can browse every span, see LLM inputs and outputs, inspect tool call arguments, and visualize the entire execution tree.

Phoenix was originally designed for production ML monitoring, but it works perfectly for local development — and it’s the best free option I’ve found for this use case.

## Prerequisites

You’ll need:

   Python 3.11+
   uv — fast Python package manager (`pip install uv` or check the uv docs)
   Docker (or Podman with Compose)
   Ollama installed and running [...] ## Wrapping Up

The setup takes about 20 minutes:

1.   `docker run` to start Phoenix
2.   `ollama pull` to get the model
3.   `uv sync` to install dependencies
4.   Three lines of instrumentation code
5.   Open `localhost:6006` and run your agent

What you get is genuine visibility into every step of your agent’s reasoning — which tools it called, what it said to them, what the LLM was thinking, and exactly where time was spent.

If you’re building with local LLMs, this is the observability stack I’d recommend starting with.

The project:beeai-framework-py-starter — clone it and follow the README. The observability example is `beeai_framework_starter/agent_observe.py`.

Arize Phoenix:github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix — open source, actively maintained, no account required for local use. [...] ## BeeAI Framework

BeeAI is an open-source agent framework from IBM. It supports multiple agent types — `ToolCallingAgent` for straightforward tool use, `RequirementAgent` for constrained orchestration where you define rules like "always call the ThinkTool first" or "call DuckDuckGo only after checking weather." It also supports multi-agent workflows where specialised agents hand off work to each other.

The framework is built on Python’s `asyncio` and integrates natively with OpenTelemetry via the OpenInference instrumentation package.

The product splits in two.

Phoenix is the free, self-hostable eval and observability tool, built on OpenInference and OpenTelemetry. Read its license before you assume it is open source: Phoenix is Elastic License 2.0, so you can run it internally at no cost but you cannot offer it as a service. Arize AX is the commercial platform: span, trace, and session evals at scale, pre-production testing of prompts and harnesses, and Alyx, an AI engineering agent that runs evals and debugs issues from inside your coding environment (Cursor and Claude Code included). [...] Best for: teams who want tracing, evals, prompt versioning, and monitoring running on their own hardware without a procurement conversation to get started.

Docs: Opik documentation · pricing · source

Pricing: free open-source version, free cloud tier with no credit card, paid enterprise tier.

## 2. Braintrust

Braintrust is built for the eval loop and opinionated about it. Run experiments against real datasets, compare prompts and models side by side, score with LLMs or code or humans. There is no open-source build, so unlike Opik and Langfuse you cannot read or fork it. You can still run the data plane in your own cloud on a commercial plan and keep your traces there. [...] That is Comet’s line, and the open-source half of it is the part worth pinning down. The Apache-2.0 build ships the backend too, so you self-host the whole platform. It carries tracing, evaluation, prompt and agent optimization, guardrails, and production monitoring with online evaluation rules. One thing is clearly outside it: Ollie, the agent that analyzes your traces and recommends fixes, needs Enterprise if you self-host. A free cloud tier including Ollie sits alongside, capped at 25k spans a month.

This approach helps catch regressions before they reach users.

### Section 9: Production Monitoring and Observability

Passing an evaluation dataset doesn't guarantee that an application will behave perfectly in production.

Real users introduce inputs and situations that developers may never have anticipated. This is why production monitoring matters.

For LLM applications, monitoring should go beyond basic server metrics. You should track:

### Application Metrics

 Request volume.
 Error rates.
 Response latency.
 API availability.

### LLM Metrics

 Token consumption.
 Model response time.
 API failures.
 Cost per request.

### Quality Metrics [...] 11.2 Promptfoo

An open-source option for testing prompts, comparing model outputs, checking assertions, running security evaluations, and integrating tests into CI/CD.

11.3 LangSmith

Provides datasets, experiments, offline and online evaluations, tracing, and feedback workflows for LLM applications and agents.

11.4 Arize Phoenix

An open-source platform for LLM observability, tracing, evaluation, and debugging. It also supports OpenTelemetry-based instrumentation.

Useful for evaluating RAG applications through metrics such as faithfulness, context precision, and context recall.

leads.content:
### Best Practices for Prompt Evaluation

- Treat prompts as versioned assets
- Design representative and diverse test datasets
- Track metrics over time, not once
- Gate production releases on evaluation thresholds
- Optimize prompts before scaling models
- Monitor cost as a first-class signal

### Final Thoughts

Prompts are code.

And like any production code, they require:

- Tests
- Metrics
- Monitoring
- Optimization pipelines

Prompt evaluation is the difference between:

> “It seems to work”

and

> “We know it works—and we can prove why.”

As GenAI systems scale, governance, reliability, and cost control will matter more than clever prompting. A robust Prompt Evaluation Framework is how teams move from experimentation to engineering discipline. [...] # From Guesswork to Governance: Building a Production-Grade Prompt Evaluation Framework

As Large Language Models (LLMs) move from experimentation into production-critical systems, one reality becomes unavoidable:

Prompt engineering without evaluation is guesswork.

Teams often invest significant effort in crafting prompts, yet rely on manual trial-and-error, subjective judgment, and anecdotal testing. This approach does not scale—and it fails silently when prompts regress, costs spike, or outputs become unreliable.

To address this gap, we built a Prompt Evaluation Framework: a systematic, metric-driven, and automated way to test, benchmark, optimize, and monitor prompts with the same rigor we apply to models and code. [...] This post outlines the why, what, and how of prompt evaluation in real-world GenAI systems.

### Why Prompt Evaluation Is No Longer Optional

### 1. Ineffective Prompt Engineering

Problem: Prompt tuning is often manual and non-reproducible. Changes are made without knowing whether quality improved or degraded.

Solution: Automated evaluation with measurable metrics enables objective comparison, regression detection, and confidence in prompt changes.

### 2. Unpredictable LLM Outputs

Problem: Hallucinations, partial reasoning, and inconsistent answers erode trust in AI systems.

Solution: Continuous monitoring using accuracy, relevance, and coherence metrics ensures output stability over time—even as models evolve.

### 3. Output Formatting Failures

The prompt‑version, release, and risk‑tier attributes [...] When you replace the stub with a supported provider client, provider instrumentation can capture model calls and available usage metadata inside the same trace. For MLflow Tracing, replace `@` with `@` and retain the operation names and metadata schema. The objective is consistent instrumentation shape, not a model‑quality benchmark.

## Trade‑offs analysis: accuracy vs latency, cost vs throughput, and flexibility vs determinism

LLM observability is a design trade‑off, not a free add‑on. Instrumentation and evaluation can improve reliability while adding latency, cost, privacy exposure, and operational complexity. [...] Roll out LLM observability in clear phases, starting small and expanding strategically.

Start with one high‑value application where quality, cost, or risk is visible to the business. Do not begin by instrumenting every prototype.

Phase the rollout:

1.   Instrument the end‑to‑end request and its major child spans.
2.   Add latency, token, cost, and reliability metrics.
3.   Define two or three task‑specific quality evaluations.
4.   Review traces for failures and high‑cost outliers.
5.   Add production sampling and monitors.
6.   Introduce release gates and governance policies.
7.   Expand the standard to additional applications.

leads.title: A Practical Guide to Observability for LLM Applications: Logs, Traces, and Quality Metrics
leads.content:
### 4.1 Retrieval Span

The retrieval span captures metadata essential to understanding the quality and relevance of retrieved context. This includes vector store identifiers, embedding queries, top-k selection, hit distribution, and a list of retrieved documents or passages. These attributes help diagnose hallucinations attributable to poor retrieval quality.

### 4.2 Prompt Span

Prompt spans record the prompt template version, interpolated variables, rendered token count, and other contextual metadata. Tracking prompt lineage is crucial because minor template changes can produce major behavioural regressions in LLM outputs.

### 4.3 LLM Call Span [...] ### Structured logs

Logs in LLM systems must be machine-readable and schema-consistent. They should encode key information such as prompts (with sensitive components masked), model outputs, configuration parameters like temperature or model version, token usage, and any errors encountered. Structured logs allow downstream OLAP systems to efficiently filter and correlate events at scale.

### Model-Quality Metrics (LLM-QA) [...] ### 6.4 Querying Examples

Robust observability enables operational and behavioural insights such as detecting prompt regressions, correlating retrieval failures with hallucination rates, and identifying anomalous token usage patterns. These analyses support continuous model improvement cycles.

## 7. Limitations and Future Work

Despite progress, LLM evaluations remain partly subjective, especially for open-ended tasks. Factuality scoring is still model-dependent, and multi-agent systems lack standardized observability patterns. Storing complete traces can also increase storage requirements substantially. Future work should explore compression-aware trace schemas, generalized evaluation benchmarks, and cross-agent tracing standards.

## Conclusion
